lesson.title: The outer electrons

lead.text: Electrons are not spread evenly around the nucleus. They sit in layers called shells, and each shell has room for only so many electrons. The first shell, the one closest to the nucleus, holds at most 2. The second shell holds at most 8, and so does the third, for the first eighteen elements.

Electrons settle into the lowest free place, just as the audience take the nearest free seat. So the first shell fills before the second one starts, and the second fills before the third. Nitrogen has seven electrons, so it puts 2 in the first shell and the other 5 in the second.

afterFigure.text: The circles in the picture group electrons by shell. Electrons do not run along the circles like trains on a track, so a drawing like this is a way of keeping count and not a photograph of motion. Compare the two atoms: nitrogen has two shells in use and sodium has three.

lead.text: Use the filling rule from the last screen. The nearest shell takes its full share before any electron goes further out.

Now find the back row. For any atom, look for the last shell that has electrons in it. That is the outer shell, and the electrons in it are called the valence electrons. Sodium has 11 electrons, which fill the shells as 2, 8 and 1, so its outer shell is the third and it has one valence electron.

These are the electrons that matter when atoms meet. The inner electrons sit close to the nucleus and are shielded by the ones outside them. The valence electrons are the ones on the edge, so they are the ones an atom loses, gains or shares.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows phosphorus and sulfur. Phosphorus has 15 electrons, which fill the shells as 2, 8 and 5, so it has five valence electrons. Sulfur has 16 electrons, arranged 2, 8 and 6, so it has six. To count the valence electrons of an atom, fill the shells in order and read off the number in the last one.

lead.text: Oxygen has two shells in use. Fill the first, then see what remains for the outer one.

steps.headline: Neutral silicon has 14 electrons. How many are valence electrons?

workedSteps.text: The second shell takes up to 8, and no more.
The 4 left sit in the third shell, the last one used. They are the valence electrons.

steps.headline: Neutral magnesium has 12 electrons. Find its valence electrons.

workedSteps.text: Fill the second shell with 8, then see what is left.

steps.headline: Different atoms with the same back row

lead.text: Atoms of different sizes can share the same number of valence electrons. Fluorine has 9 electrons arranged 2 and 7, and chlorine has 17 electrons arranged 2, 8 and 7. Chlorine has an extra shell and so it is the larger atom, but each has seven valence electrons.

That matters because the valence electrons set the chemistry. Atoms with the same number of valence electrons react in similar ways, even when they differ in size. The periodic table is laid out so that atoms with matching outer counts fall in the same column, and so a column of the table is a family of look-alike atoms.

afterFigure.text: Compare the shells in the picture ring by ring. The inner rings differ and the outer ring holds the same number of electrons in both atoms. Whenever you want to know how an atom is likely to behave, count its valence electrons first.

lead.text: Lithium has shell counts 2 and 1. Sodium has shell counts 2, 8 and 1. One thing about them matches.

steps.headline: When the outer shell is full

lead.text: Some atoms have an outer shell that is completely full. Neon has 10 electrons arranged as 2 and 8, so both of its shells are full. Argon, with 18 electrons arranged as 2, 8 and 8, is full too. Atoms like these hardly react with anything.

A full outer shell is the state that other atoms seem to head for. An atom with one or two electrons in its outer shell can reach it by giving them away, and an atom one or two short can get there by taking some. This idea drives the next lessons. It also shows why the first shell is special, since it is complete with a smaller number of electrons than the others.

diagram.alt: Neon and argon drawn as nuclei inside rings for shells with dots for electrons. Neon has 2 electrons in its first shell and 8 in its second. Argon has 2, 8 and 8 in three shells. Every shell in use is full, and the outer electrons are coloured.
diagram.caption: Each ring is a shell and each dot an electron. The coloured dots are the valence electrons. In both atoms every shell in use is full.

blocks.text: A small theatre has three rows of seats. The front row has 2 seats, the second row has 8 and the third row has 8. The audience arrive one at a time, and each person takes the nearest free seat to the stage. When nine people have come in, the front row is full and the other seven are in the second row. The third row is still empty.

Atoms seat their electrons in much the same way. Electrons stay as close to the nucleus as they can, and they sit in layers with only so many places in each. The last lesson showed that electrons can leave an atom or arrive at one, and the question now is which ones. In the theatre, the person in the back row is the one nearest the exit. In an atom, the electrons in the outermost layer turn out to be the ones that move.
This lesson seats the electrons of real atoms from the front backwards, and then looks at who ends up in the back row.

diagram.alt: A theatre seen from above with the stage at the top and three rows of seats: a front row of 2 seats, then two rows of 8. Seats fill from the front, so with nine people the front row is full, seven sit in the second row and the third row is empty.
diagram.caption: Each filled circle is a person in the nearest free seat. Use the buttons to watch the audience arrive.

intro.promise: By the end you'll place an atom's electrons in shells and pick out the outer ones.
intro.whyItMatters: The outer electrons decide how an atom behaves when it meets another atom.

recap.keyIdea: Electrons fill shells from the inside, with room for 2 in the first and 8 in each of the next two. The electrons in the last occupied shell are the valence electrons, and they decide how an atom behaves.

blocks.text: Back at the theatre, the seating rule was the same one atoms use. You filled the shells for silicon and magnesium in order and read the valence electrons off the last shell. You also saw that atoms of different sizes can have the same back row, and that neon's last shell comes out full.

recap.nextHook: Atoms whose back row is nearly empty or nearly full can lose or gain electrons easily. The next lesson pairs them up and works out the formula of the compound they make.

questions.prompt: Neutral oxygen has 8 electrons. With 2 in its first shell, how many are in its outer shell?
hints: Remove the filled first shell from the total.
Only the first shell is inside the outer shell for oxygen.
Calculate 8 − 2.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Two electrons fill the first shell, and the other six are in the outer shell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first shell, which is full and sits inside the outer shell.
That is the total. Two of the eight are in the first shell, which is inside the outer one.

questions.prompt: Neutral neon has 10 electrons. How many valence electrons does it have?
hints: Identify the outermost occupied shell.
Two of neon's electrons belong to its first shell.
Calculate 10 − 2.
questions.onCorrect: 8. Neon's shells hold 2 and 8, so the outer shell is full.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the inner shell. The valence electrons are in the last one.
That is every electron. Two of them are in the inner shell.

questions.prompt: Lithium has shell counts 2, 1 and sodium has 2, 8, 1. What matches?
hints: Compare the last occupied shell of each atom.
Count the electrons in that shell for lithium and for sodium.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each has one electron in its outermost shell.

questions.onCorrect: Each has one electron in its outermost shell. The shell number differs, but the valence count matches.

misconceptions.feedback: Lithium has two shells and sodium has three, so they differ.
Lithium has 3 electrons and sodium 11, so they differ.

questions.prompt: How many electrons fill helium's only shell?
hints: Helium occupies the first shell only.
The first shell holds a maximum of two electrons.
Count the pair in helium's only shell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first shell is full with two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Helium's only shell is the first, and it holds at most two electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the capacity of the second shell. Helium has only a first shell.

questions.prompt: Neutral aluminium has 13 electrons arranged 2, 8, 3. How many are valence electrons?
hints: Use the final occupied group.
Ignore the two inner occupied groups.
Read the population of the last occupied shell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The outermost occupied shell contains three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Only the last occupied group counts, and aluminium's holds three.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second shell, which is inside the outer one.
That is every electron. Most are in the inner shells.

questions.prompt: What do the circles in this atom drawing represent?
hints: Use the drawing as a model of shell populations.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They group electrons for counting; actual electrons occupy quantum states.

questions.onCorrect: The circles group electrons by shell, to make counting easy. They are not paths that electrons follow.

misconceptions.feedback: Electrons do not move along circles. The drawing only groups them.
The circles are not surfaces. They group electrons by shell.

questions.prompt: How many people are in the second row?
hints: Which row fills first, and how many does it take?
Take those people off the total.
Do the remaining people fit in the second row, or do they spill into the third?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 people remain, and the second row holds up to 8, so all 7 sit there.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The front row fills first and the rest go to the next row. Electrons fill shells in the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is everyone. The first row takes some of them.
That is how many the second row could hold. Only the people left over sit there.

questions.prompt: A neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons. How many are in its second shell?
hints: Which shell fills first, and how many does it take?
Take those electrons off the total.
Does the second shell have room for all the rest?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 − 2 = 4, and the second shell holds up to 8.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The first shell takes 2, and the rest fit in the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every electron. Two are in the first shell.
That is the first shell. The question asks about the second.

questions.prompt: Why do the last 4 electrons of silicon go into a third shell?

acceptedIdeas: The second shell holds eight at most, so it is already full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 + 8 = 10 electrons fill the first two shells, so 4 must go further out.

choices.label: The second shell holds eight at most, so it is already full
Electrons prefer to be far from the nucleus
The third shell is always filled first

questions.onCorrect: Right: once a shell is full the next electrons go into the shell outside it.

misconceptions.feedback: Electrons fill the inner shells first. The outer shell gets what is left.
Shells fill from the inside, so the third is filled last.

questions.prompt: After filling the first shell with 2 and the second with 8, how many of magnesium's 12 electrons are left?
hints: Add up the electrons in the first two shells.
Take that total off the 12.
What is left is in the third shell.
questions.onCorrect: 2. The electrons left after the inner shells are the valence electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what is left after the first shell only. Fill the second as well.
That is the second shell's share. The question asks for what is left over.

questions.prompt: A neutral beryllium atom has 4 electrons. How many valence electrons does it have?
hints: How many electrons fit in the first shell?
Take those off the total.
Is there a second shell with electrons in it?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 − 2 = 2 left for the second shell, which is the last one used.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The first shell takes two, and the rest are the outer electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every electron. Some are in the inner shell.
That is the capacity of the second shell, not how many electrons sit in it.
